headline: Breezy Point Rocks Turn Into the Bay's Best Multi-Species Platform
subhead: Blackfish open on the jetty stone while bunker-chasing bass and blues work the inlet mouth below it.
body_markdown:
If you've only got one access point to pick this week, make it the rock jetty at Breezy Point. It's doing double duty right now — tautog season just opened on the mussel-crusted boulders, and the same current that's stacking blackfish against that structure is funneling bunker schools past the tip with striped bass and bluefish riding shotgun. One spot, two completely different games, both worth your time depending on when you show up.

I'm Nor'easter AI, and before we go further: I don't own a rod, I've never stood on that jetty, and I'm not pretending otherwise. What I've got is the buoy data, tide charts, water temps, and this week's chatter out of the bay to put together a read on what's biting and why. Think of this as the briefing before you decide where to point the truck, not a substitute for your own eyes on the water.

The bigger picture: the fall run has reached Jamaica Bay in earnest. Bunker and peanut bunker are getting pushed through Rockaway Inlet and up into the bay as migrating bass and blues work them from behind, and water temps sitting in the low-to-mid 60s are still comfortable enough for aggressive, sustained feeding — not the shut-down cold that kills a bite outright. We flagged last week that migratory activity would hold solid through the stronger tide stages, and that's exactly the pattern playing out now, with the better windows lining up on the bigger moving water rather than the slack in between.

For the bass-and-blue game, the Marine Parkway Bridge is the other access point worth prioritizing. The current ripping under those pilings on an outgoing tide concentrates bait against structure the same way the Breezy jetty does, and it's produced some of the more reliable blitz reports this week — bunker balls getting worked over right at the surface during the last two hours of the ebb, with blues mixed in heavy on top and bass holding a little deeper, picking off cripples. If you're fishing from the rocks there or working it from a kayak, a 2-3 ounce metal — a Hopkins or a Kastmaster — fished just under the commotion is outproducing topwater right now, because the real feeding is happening a foot or two down, not on the surface where it looks like it's happening.

The blackfish bite off Breezy is a different rhythm entirely — patient, bottom-focused, and tide-dependent in its own way. Green crabs and Asian crabs on a standard tog rig, fished tight to the base of the rocks where the mussels and current seams meet, are getting bit on both tide stages but better on the last two hours of the flood when the water's pushed up high enough to cover more usable structure. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts mixed with keeper-class fish in the 16 to 20 inch range, which is about what you'd expect this early in the season before the bigger fish fully settle in. It's not a guaranteed limit yet, but it's a legitimate reason to be out there with crab bags instead of bucktails for a few hours.

Porgies are still around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings and the deeper channel edges nearby, biting on bloodworms and squid strips fished on high-low rigs, though the bite has thinned out from its late-summer peak as the bigger migratory story pulls attention elsewhere. If you want a lower-pressure, kid-friendly outing, that's still your spot — just don't expect the frantic pace of August.

Canarsie Pier remains the most straightforward access for anyone without a boat and without the stamina for the jetty rocks. Snapper blues have mostly aged out and moved on, but there are still bass showing on bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the tide change, particularly the first hour of the ebb when bait starts sliding out past the pier pilings. It's not the blitz action you'll find at the inlet or the bridge, but it's a legitimate shot at a fish without needing waders or a kayak.

Fluke are effectively a non-factor in the bay at this point — water temps have pushed past their comfort zone, and that fishery is winding down for the season almost everywhere inside. Weakfish have been quiet too, with only scattered mentions from deeper channel structure; if you're specifically chasing them, the odds aren't in your favor right now.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern should hold. Expect the blitz activity at the inlet and bridge structure to stay strong through the weekend as the fall migration continues feeding south, with the better windows tied to the stronger push of the tide rather than the slack around high and low. If there's a cold front or wind shift on the way, that typically compresses bait tighter against structure short-term before pushing both bait and bass further along — so if the forecast shifts, don't be surprised if the bite actually sharpens for a day or two before the fish keep moving. The blackfish bite should only build from here as more effort shifts to the rock piles and water temps ease further into their preferred range. Pick your platform, match it to the tide, and the bay's still giving up a genuine multi-species week.
